## Architecture

**Rust decides, AVFoundation and Metal do** (spec §7). The core holds the
project (JSON, spec §5.2), every edit, the composition plan, the per-frame
recipe, the index of a WebM/Matroska file being imported and the WebM file an
`av1_webm`, `vp9_webm` or `vp9_alpha_webm` export writes (its container only; the packets come from Swift). Swift owns windows, gestures, undo, AVFoundation playback and export,
the Metal compositor, media import and its caches and on-device analysis of
the media (Vision and Sound Analysis on the analysis lane, cached per media
in `cache/analysis/`; the core reads only what a tool or op hands it), and
agent dispatch. No
pixel or sample work in Rust; no ffmpeg dependency in the product. The AV1 and
VP9 encoders (SVT-AV1, libvpx; `designs/adr/codec-export.md`) are
platform-side like AVFoundation: Swift calls them through the bridging header,
no `rc_*` export wraps them (spec §11 CX-4).

### FFI contract

- `core/include/framejob_core.h` is a **hand-maintained** C header, the single
  contract between the worlds. **The FFI is three files in lockstep**: a Rust
  `#[no_mangle]` export, its entry in the header, and its wrapper in
  `app/Sources/ReelCore.swift` and its `ReelCore+<Area>.swift` files, **the
  only files that call `rc_*`** (spec §11 CJ-8 (l)); a new wrapper goes in
  the file of its area.
- A handle is an immutable project. **Every edit is pure and answers one of
  three arms** (`core/src/outcome.rs`, spec §5.5): applied with the new
  project, an identity, or refused in the rule's own sentence. Only the first
  is an undo step. `ProjectDocument` is the single mutation point and undo is
  its stack of handles.
- Edits are JSON ops through `rc_project_apply`. **The op table is two
  halves**: what an op MEANS is the module doc of `core/src/edit.rs`, and
  what it TAKES — every argument's name, kind and required-ness — is
  `core/src/op_table.rs`, as data, published as JSON Schema by
  `rc_op_schemas`. `ReelOps.swift`'s typed builders,
  `AgentCatalog*.swift`'s tools and spec §6 mirror them — change one, change
  all four — **except that every op TOOL prints the arguments half instead of
  restating it** (`AgentCatalog.opTool`), so an argument added to an op costs
  a sentence of prose there and no schema. A tool that takes more or less
  than its op does says so in `AgentCatalog+Declarations.swift`, one row and
  one reason each. The envelope's `scope` key addresses an edit inside a
  nest.
- Persisted-state changes bump `RC_FORMAT_VERSION` in `core/src/format.rs`
  **and** the header.
- Errors: `rc_project_apply` returns NULL three distinguishable ways, and the
  two message channels are never both written. NULL with NEITHER written is
  an identity; NULL with `reason_out` set is a refusal and that string is the
  rule's own sentence; NULL with `err_out` set is invalid input. The first two
  make no undo step and only the third is an error. `"internal error: …"` is a
  caught panic.

### Where a feature lands — the standard recipe

Every shipped feature follows the same shape; putting a step's code anywhere
else is what bloats files:

1. **Core:** the op's semantics in an `impl Project` block in the module of
   its own concern (a new concern is a new module); the row in `edit.rs`'s
   enum and module-doc table, and its arguments in `op_table.rs` (which is
   where `OP_NAMES` comes from); a persisted field with a serde default and a
   `schema_vN.rs`; a new `core/tests/*.rs`. A field lands in the same phase as
   the thing that renders it.
2. **FFI**, only when a new `rc_*` export is needed: Rust → header →
   the ReelCore file of its area.
3. **Swift:** the typed builder in `ReelOps.swift`; a small value or model
   file; an `EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift` with its validator arm; an
   inspector section REGISTERED in `ClipPane.makeSections()`; a menu item in
   `AppDelegate+Menus.swift`; a gesture as a session struct.
4. **MCP mirror:** a handler in `AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`, a catalog entry
   declaring `scope`, and a comment naming the UI path it mirrors.
5. **Documents:** spec §5.2 / §6 / §7.10 for anything they mirror; the map
   entry in the per-side `CLAUDE.md` if a file's role changed; the feature's
   page in `docs/guide/` (and its README highlight and
   `menus-and-shortcuts.md` row when it adds one); the phase's record in its
   road map.
6. **Verify:** as "Verification" below says; then read the change back
   adversarially before committing.

## Rules

- Conventions are Rasterize's — `~/devel/rasterize`'s three `CLAUDE.md`
  files are the parent text for anything not settled here.
- **Every user-visible edit gets an MCP mirror** (spec §7.9): a handler, a
  catalog entry, and a comment naming the UI path. The startup parity check
  in `AgentServer.prepareCatalog()` has SIX parts: catalog names against handler
  names, every op in the core's table against the tools (through
  `rc_op_names`, with an explicit allow-list for ops that deliberately have
  none), each tool's schema shape, that every op tool declares `scope`,
  that every op tool declares the CORE's own arguments for its op — each one
  described, and no description for an argument no op has
  (`AgentServer+Parity.swift`), and that every tool `ModelKeys.keyed` names
  exists and its description carries its key's clause
  (`AgentServer+Parity.swift`, spec §11 CJ-13). What it cannot see is a CALL, which two
  things guard at dispatch: the argument GATE in `AgentServer+Gate.swift`
  compares the caller's keys to the schema the tool published and refuses a
  stranger by name, for all one hundred and twenty-five product tools (and the dev tools,
  road map 11), before any handler runs;
  and the throwing helpers in `AgentServer+Arguments.swift` refuse a value a
  handler cannot read by name rather than dropping it.
- **A feature that needs a language or cloud model tests its key through
  `ModelKeys`** (spec §11 CJ-3): presence, the sentence, the control's or
  menu item's mark, the tool's refusal where it would send, and a row in
  `ModelKeys.keyed`.
- **A file at the ~600-line cap gives something up before it takes anything
  on**, as a pure move landed and gated alone; new files are capped at 400
  lines. Frozen files take wiring only. `core/src/edit.rs` and
  `app/Sources/ReelOps.swift` are exempt (tables, one row per op), and proof
  instruments in `tools/proof/` are held to neither cap. The ledger is
  `wc -l app/Sources/*.swift core/src/*.rs graphic/src/*.rs | sort -rn`; the
  seam a record already named for a file is under "Named next cuts" in
  `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` / `core-file-history.md`.
- **Size rules are per FILE, never per feature.** A brief, design, road map,
  spec or proof never sets a budget on how many lines a feature may add,
  never measures a feature's total against one, and never names code size as
  a reason to cut, trim or drop a feature: a feature takes as much code as it
  needs. Keeping files small is the cap above and its pure moves, nothing
  else (owner, 2026-10-10).
- **A decision in spec §11 is not re-litigated** (`designs/spec/11-decisions/`). A phase that needs a new
  one records it there before the code, not after.
- **`.secrets/` (gitignored) holds the owner's own keys for proofs**, e.g.
  `.secrets/anthropic-key`, read ONLY by `anthropic_key()` in
  `tools/proof/assistant_prompt_eval.py`. Never open, print, grep, copy or
  list its contents; never move a key from it into an argument, the
  environment of a build, a log or a file. A run that spends money still
  needs its explicit flags (`--live --cap <dollars>`); the file's presence
  spends nothing. Every paid proof request is also held to the month's
  budget (spec §11 P-3, P-6) in
  `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job Proofs/spend.jsonl`; an agent
  never edits it, raises a budget, or points a verification at it.
- **A check only a person at the machine can make is a row in
  `docs/manual-checks.md`**, added in the change that creates it — never a
  `ready-for-human` issue, and never an instrument built to stand in for the
  person (how a pane looks, whether audio plays, a real key's conversation).
  Automate what a script can truly measure; list only the residue.
- Commit only when asked. A commit message says what was verified and what
  is owed, and the road map's record says the same.

## Verifying a build

A local Distribution build is only ever checked, never launched: it loads
Sparkle, which library validation refuses in an ad-hoc signed hardened app
(spec §11 PUB-7). Debug and Release link with `-dead_strip_dylibs`, so they
never load it.

The app is verified by driving the built binary over MCP and comparing what
it renders — not by reading code. Launch your own instance on your own socket
and only ever kill that one (`pgrep -f "MacOS/Frame Job"` lists them, Debug
and Release alike; the products folder tells them apart; another session may
have one running):

```sh
make app-debug
python3 tools/proof/proof_app.py launch   # prints folder, socket, log, pid
```

Each later command names the printed folder literally
(`mcp.MCP("<dir>/agent.sock")`, `python3 tools/proof/phaseN_proof.py
<dir>/agent.sock`, `grep "Frame Job: " <dir>/framejob.log`), because a shell
variable does not survive from one agent command to the next; stop it by the
pid the launcher prints.

The log line `Frame Job agent socket listening at <dir>/agent.sock` says it is
up (`not bound: <reason>` says why not). Drive it with `tools/proof/mcp.py`'s
`mcp.MCP("<dir>/agent.sock")` (streamable HTTP over the Unix socket), or with
the bundled stdio helper `framejob-mcp` with `RC_AGENT_SOCKET` set to the same
path: one tool per §6 op, each taking the `scope`
envelope key, plus the app-state tools — `open_project`, `new_project`,
`new_project_from_range`, `save_project`, `close_project`, `get_project`, `import_media`,
`import_captions`, `export_captions`, `transcribe`, `consolidate_media`, `detect_silence`,
`detect_fillers`, `transcribe_for_fillers`, `get_transcript`, `get_timeline_transcript`, `get_media_analysis`, `split_at_shots`, `normalize_clip`, `enhance_voice`, `match_audio`, `set_playhead`, `set_range`, `set_selection`, `set_scope`,
`undo`, `redo`, `render_frame`, `export`, `export_status`, `auto_zoom`, `add_shortcut_overlays`, `speed_up_typing`, `cancel_export`,
`record_screen`, `write_graphic`,
`get_graphic`, `graphic_reference`, `render_graphic`, `import_graphic_font`,
`import_graphic_asset`, `delete_graphic`, `rename_graphic`,
`restore_graphic`, `list_graphics`, `insert_graphic`, `export_graphic` and `import_graphic`. A Debug or Release build also has the dev tools
(`snapshot_ui`, `perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`;
"Seeing the chrome" below; `play_preview`, which plays a window's preview
for a while and answers the frames composed (#127, spec §11 G-36);
`graphic_memory`, which answers the graphic rasters' memory budget, what is
held and kept, and simulates memory pressure (G-37); `loudness_meter`, which
answers a window's live loudness meter (momentary, short-term, integrated,
true peak, the frames measured and its resets) and resets it (road map
"audio" AP7, AU-77); `land_recording`, which lands fixture files as a
finished recording through the recorder panel's door or `record_screen`'s,
so a proof can watch Enhance the microphone when it lands without a
microphone grant (spec §11 AU-69); and
`analysis_job`, which wants a media's analysis under a document's stand-in
owner and returns at once, or waits for every such job and answers their
runs (spec §11 CJ-27); and `-RCDevAnalysisHold <s>`, which holds each
analysis job before its first frame, polling cancellation, so a proof can
act during it; and `-RCDevAnalysisCanned YES`, with which a canned analysis
marker is honoured (spec §11 CJ-26); and `transcript_view`, which answers

A proof picks its app through `tools/proof/proof_app.py`: `RC_PROOF_APP` is
`debug` (the default), `release` or a `.app` path. `mcp.launch`, `mcp.MCP` and
`python3 tools/proof/proof_app.py launch` refuse a tree's built app when any
input is newer than its last complete build (its
`_CodeSignature/CodeResources`), or an instance started before an input
changed, naming the file, its time and the `make` target.

Release-only proofs pass `release_only=` (`git grep release_only= tools/proof`);
recording_proof's socket instance is started with
`python3 tools/proof/proof_app.py launch --app release`.

**Before trusting any MCP proof, `grep "Frame Job: " <dir>/framejob.log`
must print nothing** — that prefix is the startup parity check complaining.
On a Debug build the same complaint is an `assertionFailure` that traps first
(`AgentServer.prepareCatalog`), so `make app-debug` fails at Write Agent
Catalog with `Fatal error: …` instead of logging the line.

A proof's instance shares its bundle's defaults domain (the owner's
`com.kgalligan.FrameJob` for a Release build, `com.kgalligan.FrameJob.debug`
for a Debug build, spec §11 V-5): no
environment moves `UserDefaults` (#238). Never perform a persisting menu item
(View ▸ Snapping, Safe Areas, Hide Inspector, Timeline Track Height, Preview
Quality) on either build: `mcp.py` ends the script with status 3 and
`DEFAULTS MOVED` last on stderr when its session moved a key and no other
Frame Job shares the domain, and only prints the line when one does;
`defaults_proof.py` is its proof. The guard reads the domain with
`CFFIXED_USER_HOME` taken out of `defaults`' environment
(`proof_defaults.read_env`), so a proof run under a scratch home that does
not exist yet, or is removed before the script ends, is compared with
itself: `defaults export` answers no key under a variable naming an absent
folder.

**`tools/proof/` holds the scripts that do this** — an MCP script per phase
over a dependency-free client (`mcp.py`), and beside most of them an
offscreen-chrome script or a probe. Every claim in them is a placement read
back through `get_project`, a BYTE comparison of two PNGs, or a
sample-for-sample comparison of two exports decoded to PCM (which needs
`ffmpeg` at proof time). Its README says how to make the test media, run
one, and which scores are known host-state skips (a locked console, a
Bluetooth output). Add the next phase's proof there rather than writing a
throwaway. An instance DEADLOCKS somewhere past forty documents open at once:
a proof that closes what it opens (`close_project`) can share an instance, and
one that does not relaunches between proof sessions.

Spec §10's per-step verifications are the acceptance tests. What no script
can answer — step 4's "the clip plays with audio", step 5's 60 fps, and the
rest — is a row in `docs/manual-checks.md`, which the owner runs.

## Verification

- **In the loop:** a targeted test (`cd core && cargo test --release --test
  <file> <filter>`), `make lint` after Rust edits, `make typecheck` after Swift
  edits, `make app-debug` before driving the app, and the phase's own rows
  (`--only` where the proof has it) against Debug.
- **Once, when the code is complete:** `make gate`, in the foreground, under
  the 600 s tool cap (`make gate GATE_ARGS=--force` only when a stamp itself is
  in doubt). It stops at the first failure and skips a step whose inputs and
  tools are byte-identical to its last pass, so after a fix it re-runs only
  what the fix can change. Never run one of its steps by hand to stand in for
  it, never re-run an unchanged step, and never run anything twice with no
  edit between.
- **The proof a phase records** runs whole once, on the final instrument,
  against Release (`RC_PROOF_APP=release` after the gate's `make app`), with
  any `release_only` proof the change touches. This is a rule: nothing checks
  which build a recorded run drove.
- **A proof that fails only on Debug** is pinned `release_only="<reason>"` in
  the change that finds it (spec §11 V-4); an assert trap on Debug is a defect
  to fix, never a pin.
- **Mutants** target the decisions the phase adds: about one per new branch,
  threshold, refusal or ordering, usually 3–8; more than 10 only with a reason
  written in the spec. The full set runs once, at the end, on the final
  instrument.
- **A fix pass** re-runs only the rows whose instrument code it changed and
  the mutants whose anchor lines it touched, then `make gate`.
- **Background** only for a command that cannot fit 600 s, waited on once with
  a bound; never a poll loop.

## Seeing the chrome

`screencapture` needs a Screen Recording grant the agent's terminal may or
may not have (it varies by host and session), and without it `screencapture`
silently writes a black PNG. Assume neither: a proof that needs the grant
probes for it and skips its granted tier by name, and a capture is never
trusted until it is checked non-black. The way to LOOK at the chrome is
**`tools/proof/harness/`**: it compiles every file in `app/Sources` except
`main.swift` with a `main.swift` of its own, links the staticlib, opens a
`.framejob` package, puts an `EditorViewController` in an `NSWindow` and
`cacheDisplay`s it into a PNG at the display's backing scale — the same paint
path the window uses, no TCC grant, either appearance, captured on SETTLE.
The preview well comes out as the canvas background (an `AVPlayerLayer` or
Metal layer does not draw into `cacheDisplay`), so nothing about the PICTURE
is ever claimed offscreen; pixel claims go over MCP. `tools/proof/README.md`'s
"offscreen harness" section has the build line, the argument list and the
pinned `UserDefaults`.

To look at the LIVE app, a Debug or Release build (`make app-debug`,
`make app`; never Distribution) has dev tools over MCP (road map 11, spec §11 V-1).
`snapshot_ui` captures the editor, a sheet, Settings, Welcome or the recorder panel, with a
layout dump. `perform_menu_item` runs a menu item by path to put a sheet or
Settings up, `cancel_sheet` closes the sheet, and `select_inspector_tab`
picks an inspector tab and sub-tab. All four work with the
app inactive and its window covered. A capture's look is set at launch with
the dev-only `-RCDevAppearance light|dark`, never switched live. To see every
catalogued screen at once, `python3 tools/proof/screens.py` walks
`designs/screens/`, once per look, each time on its own pinned instance. It
writes each screen's PNGs and layout dumps and one `screens.md` with the
prose and each capture's layout problems. The last screen is the recorder
panel: shown from the background it no longer takes key (#137), but an
instance that is active when it runs still gets a key panel with Record on
Return, so the script stops each instance straight after capturing it.

Two rules from it worth carrying into any proof: **identical, stable,
DIFFERENT output across processes is an Auto Layout ambiguity to find, not a
race to out-wait** — reach for constraint priorities, not for more run-loop
turns (on an `NSStackView` that is `setHuggingPriority(_:for:)`;
`setContentHuggingPriority` is inert on a stack); and **when the thing to
check is app ARITHMETIC or app STRUCTURE with
no caller a script can reach** (a menu, a validator, a cue builder, a queue),
the answer is a probe compiled from `app/Sources` through
`tools/proof/swift_build.py`, not a photograph. A probe that will not build is a scored
FAILURE, never an exit, so a rotted instrument cannot take a score down with
it. **That rule applies to historical instruments too.** The meter and welcome
comparisons build old `app/Sources` with the matching old core and header in
isolated output directories, using the current guarded `harness/main.swift`
for both paints; `cloud_captions_probe.py`'s W and SP baselines build the
same way through `reference_build.py`, each in its own folder. A failed current or reference build is a scored failure,
including an FFI diagnostic; it is never a historical skip or a reason to
fall back to the old harness. Only the recording proof's granted tier can
skip rows for a named host condition such as a locked console.

content.content:
# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, and `engines` in `package.json` sets the Node it needs. `README.md` has
the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

## blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).

---
title: "How edits work"
description: What an edit acts on, why clips never push each other, and the rules every timeline edit keeps.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Every edit in Frame Job acts on something you've already pointed at, and every edit keeps the same few rules. Once you know them, you can tell what a command will touch and why one sometimes won't go through.

Most commands act on the selected clips. Some also use the playhead, the in and out range or the current track.

| **The playhead** | The moment you're looking at. | Split, trim to the playhead, Freeze Frame, Paste, Insert and Overwrite at Playhead |
| **The in and out range** | The stretch between the points set with <kbd>I</kbd> and <kbd>O</kbd>. <kbd>⌥X</kbd> clears both. See [The in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/). | With nothing selected, Delete and Ripple Delete act on the range |

---
title: "Delete, Ripple Delete and Lift"
description: "Remove clips or a stretch of the timeline, and choose whether the hole stays open or closes up."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

There are two delete keys, and the difference between them is what happens to the hole. <kbd>⌫</kbd> leaves it open, so everything else keeps its timing. <kbd>⌘⌫</kbd> closes it, so the rest of the timeline moves left.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['Edit ▸ Delete', 'Edit ▸ Ripple Delete']}
  keys={['⌫', '⌘⌫']}
  where="The Ripple Delete button in the timeline bar"
  tools={['delete', 'ripple_delete', 'lift_range', 'ripple_delete_range', 'ripple_delete_ranges']}
/>

## Choose a delete

Each key acts on the selection, or on the [in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/) when nothing is selected.

| | Clips selected | Nothing selected, a range set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <kbd>⌫</kbd> **Edit ▸ Delete** | **Delete:** removes the clips and leaves gaps. | **Lift:** removes what's in the range and moves nothing. |
| <kbd>⌘⌫</kbd> **Edit ▸ Ripple Delete** | **Ripple Delete:** removes the clips and closes each hole. | **Ripple Delete:** removes what's in the range and closes the hole. |

A selection takes priority over a range, so [deselect](/timeline/selecting-clips/) first to act on the range. An empty range is ignored. With nothing to remove, both menu items are greyed out and the keys beep.

## Delete clips and leave a gap

Select the clips and press <kbd>⌫</kbd>. They go, the gaps stay, and nothing else moves. It's one undo step, named Delete.

- A picture takes its [linked sound](/audio/detach-and-attach/) with it, unless the sound's track is locked.
- A linked sound clip goes alone, and leaves its picture silent.
- A clip on a locked track that you selected by clicking is still removed.

21	=================== how-edits-work
22	---
23	title: "How edits work"
24	description: What an edit acts on, why clips never push each other, and the rules every timeline edit keeps.
25	---
26	
27	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
28	
29	Every edit in Frame Job acts on something you've already pointed at, and every edit keeps the same few rules. Once you know them, you can tell what a command will touch and why one sometimes won't go through.
30	
31	<AtAGlance
32	  menu={['Mark ▸ Set In', 'Mark ▸ Set Out', 'Mark ▸ Clear Range']}
33	  keys={['I', 'O', '⌥X']}
34	  where="The timeline: the selection, the playhead and the range"
35	  tools={['set_selection', 'set_playhead', 'set_range']}
36	/>
37	
38	## What an edit acts on
39	
40	Most commands act on the selected clips. Some also use the playhead, the in and out range or the current track.
41	
42	| What | What it is | What uses it |
43	| --- | --- | --- |
44	| **The selection** | The clips outlined in coral on the timeline. See [Select clips](/timeline/selecting-clips/). | Most commands |
45	| **The playhead** | The moment you're looking at. | Split, trim to the playhead, Freeze Frame, Paste, Insert and Overwrite at Playhead |
46	| **The in and out range** | The stretch between the points set with <kbd>I</kbd> and <kbd>O</kbd>. <kbd>⌥X</kbd> clears both. See [The in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/). | With nothing selected, Delete and Ripple Delete act on the range |
47	| **The current track** | The track of the first selected clip, or the front-most track when nothing is selected. With a [nest](/editing/inside-a-nest/) open, it's a track inside the nest. | Close Gap, Select All on Track, Insert and Overwrite at Playhead |
48	
49	A selected clip's linked partner, such as its [detached sound](/audio/detach-and-attach/), shows a dashed ring. Most edits take it along, as long as its track isn't locked.
50	
51	## Clips never push each other
52	
53	A clip you drag never shoves its neighbours out of the way. A place that would need a neighbour to move isn't available, so the clip [stops short of it](/editing/move-clips/#when-a-drop-wont-go-where-you-let-go).
54	
55	Only the edits that are there to move other clips do so: [Ripple Delete](/editing/delete-clips/), [Close Gap](/editing/close-gaps/), [Insert](/editing/insert-and-overwrite/#insert-a-file), [inserting time](/editing/close-gaps/#insert-time), [Freeze Frame](/speed/freeze-frame/) and [Retime Range](/speed/retime-range/). They open or close time across every unlocked track. A [locked track](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/) stays where it is.
56	
57	## The overlap rule
58	
59	Two clips on one track may overlap a little, and that overlap is a [transition](/motion/transitions/). The rule has three parts:
60	
61	- A clip can overlap at most one neighbour on each side.
62	- Each overlap can be at most half the length of the shorter clip.
63	- An adjustment clip can't overlap another clip at all, because it can't take a transition. Fade it with opacity instead.
64	
65	An edit that leaves a clip overlapping the clip before it gives that clip a Cross Dissolve over the overlap, unless it already has a transition.
66	
67	Moves, trims, nudges, duplicates, gap closes and nests won't break the rule. Paste and Un-nest put a clip that would break it on a new track at the front instead. The rule never stops a ripple delete: a clip it slides onto a neighbour gets a Cross Dissolve.
68	
69	## Times land on frames
70	
71	Every time you give an edit, by dragging or typing, lands on a whole frame of the project's [frame rate](/projects/frame-rate/). A moved or trimmed clip goes to the nearest frame, so you can't place a clip between two frames. A time before the start of the timeline stops at 0.
72	
73	The exceptions are the short audio times typed in the **Sound** sub-tab, such as a fade length or a compressor's attack, which keep the value you typed. A fade dragged by its handle on the clip still lands on a frame.
74	
75	A move or a ripple shifts every clip by exactly the same amount, so clips stay in step. At a frame rate that doesn't divide evenly, such as 7 fps, a shifted start can sit off the frame grid by a sliver too small to see.
76	
77	## One frame minimum
78	
79	[Trims](/editing/trimming/) and [rolls](/editing/slip-and-roll/) always leave a clip at least one frame long. The drag stops there, however far you pull.
80	
81	## Project limits
82	
83	| A project holds up to | |
84	| --- | --- |
85	| Clips | 4,096 |
86	| Tracks | 64 |
87	| Levels of nesting | 8 |
88	| Markers | 1,024 |
89	| Media files | 1,024 |
90	
91	Clips and tracks inside nests count towards the same totals as the ones on the timeline. An edit that would pass a limit doesn't happen, and the project stays as it was. See [Limits](/reference/limits/).
92	
93	## When an edit doesn't go through
94	
95	Frame Job beeps, changes nothing and adds no undo step. When a rule stopped the edit, the reason appears at the foot of the inspector. An edit that would change nothing beeps too, with no reason given. An edit Frame Job can't carry out at all, such as placing a file shorter than one frame or passing a project limit, shows an alert instead of a beep.
96	
97	A drag is quieter. It stays at the last position the project allows, with no beep. See [When an edit is refused](/getting-started/refused-edits/).
98	
99	## With an agent
100	
101	[`set_selection`](/mcp/tools-view-state/#set_selection), [`set_playhead`](/mcp/tools-view-state/#set_playhead) and [`set_range`](/mcp/tools-view-state/#set_range) set the selection, the playhead and the range. They aren't edits and they add no undo step. See [Tools: playhead, range and selection](/mcp/tools-view-state/).
102	
103	An agent's times land on frames too. A negative position on the timeline becomes 0, but a negative length is an error and nothing changes.
104	
105	## Related
106	
107	- [Core concepts](/getting-started/core-concepts/)
108	- [Select clips](/timeline/selecting-clips/)
109	- [When an edit is refused](/getting-started/refused-edits/)
110	- [Undo and saving](/getting-started/undo-and-saving/)
111	- [Hide and lock tracks](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/)
112	=================== add-clips
113	---
114	title: "Add clips to the timeline"
115	description: Drag a file from the Media tab onto a track or the canvas, and see where it lands and what stops a drop.
116	---
117	
118	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
119	
120	Importing a file puts it in the [Media tab](/projects/media-tab/), not on the timeline. To use it, drag its row onto a track or onto the preview canvas.
121	
122	<AtAGlance
123	  where={['Media tab ▸ drag a row onto a track', 'Media tab ▸ drag a row onto the preview canvas']}
124	  tools={['add_clip', 'add_track']}
125	/>
126	
127	This page covers files. [Text](/text-and-shapes/text-clips/), [shapes](/text-and-shapes/shape-clips/) and [graphics](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/) have their own ways in.
128	
129	## Drag media onto a track
130	
131	Drag a row from the Media tab onto a track. The whole file lands as one clip at the pointer, on the nearest frame, and nothing else moves. The drop doesn't snap to the edges of other clips.
132	
133	Hold a modifier as you let go to make room for the file or replace what's there. See [Insert and overwrite](/editing/insert-and-overwrite/#drop-with-a-modifier).
134	
135	A drop that overlaps a neighbour a little still lands, as long as it keeps to the [overlap rule](/editing/how-edits-work/#the-overlap-rule), and makes a Cross Dissolve over the overlap.
136	
137	**Edit ▸ Undo** names this step Add Clip.
138	
139	## Drop media on the canvas
140	
141	Drop a row on the preview canvas to add the file at the playhead, on a new track at the front. Use this to lay a file over everything else without looking for a free stretch of track.
142	
143	The new track and the clip are one undo step, Add Clip. Modifier keys do nothing here.
144	
145	## What a new clip covers
146	
147	A new clip starts at the head of the file and runs its whole length, at normal speed. The length rounds down to whole frames, so the clip never runs past the end of the file. That can leave a part of a frame at the tail unused.
148	
149	- **A picture** is 5 seconds long. [Trim it](/editing/trimming/) to any length.
150	- **A file larger than the canvas** is scaled to fit, while **Fit new clips to canvas** is on in the [Document tab](/projects/document-tab/). It's on by default. A smaller file keeps its size.
151	- **A video or sound file shorter than one frame** of the project can't be placed, and Frame Job says so.
152	
153	## When a drop doesn't land
154	
155	| What happened | What you see |
156	| --- | --- |
157	| The clip would break the [overlap rule](/editing/how-edits-work/#the-overlap-rule) | Frame Job beeps, adds nothing, and gives the reason at the foot of the inspector. Hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> to insert or <kbd>⇧⌥</kbd> to overwrite as you drop instead. |
158	| You let go above or below the lanes | The drag springs back. Only a [clip already on the timeline](/editing/move-clips/#move-a-clip-to-a-new-track) makes a new track that way. |
159	| You let go in another project's window | The drag springs back. A row can only be placed in its own project. |
160	
161	A `.cube` LUT row doesn't drag at all. [Apply it as a look](/color/luts/) instead.
162	
163	## Good to know
164	
165	- A plain drop onto a [locked track](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/) still places the clip, because nothing has to move.
166	- If the project already has 64 tracks, a drop on the canvas adds the file to the front track instead, and the overlap rule can stop it there.
167	- Files dragged from the Finder are different. On the Media tab they [import](/projects/import-media/). Anywhere else in the window, each opens as a project of its own.
168	
169	## With an agent
170	
171	[`add_clip`](/mcp/tools-adding-clips/#add_clip) places a file on a track at a time you give it, as a plain drop does, and the same rules stop it. To lay a file over everything else, as a drop on the canvas does, an agent calls [`add_track`](/mcp/tools-tracks-and-markers/#add_track) first. See [Tools: adding clips](/mcp/tools-adding-clips/).
172	
173	## Related
174	
175	- [Import media](/projects/import-media/)
176	- [Insert and overwrite](/editing/insert-and-overwrite/)
177	- [Move clips](/editing/move-clips/)
178	- [Trim clips](/editing/trimming/)
179	=================== insert-and-overwrite
180	---
181	title: "Insert and overwrite"
182	description: Bring a file into a cut that's already timed, either by making room for it or by replacing what's there.
183	---
184	
185	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
186	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
187	
188	Insert and Overwrite bring a file into a cut that's already timed. Insert makes room for it and pushes everything later along. Overwrite replaces what's there and moves nothing.
189	
190	<AtAGlance
191	  menu={['Edit ▸ Insert at Playhead', 'Edit ▸ Overwrite at Playhead']}
192	  keys={['⌥-drop', '⇧⌥-drop']}
193	  where="Right-click a row in the Media tab"
194	  tools={['insert_clip', 'overwrite_clip']}
195	/>
196	
197	## Place a file at the playhead
198	
199	<Steps>
200	
201	1. Click the file's row in the Media tab.
202	
203	2. Move the playhead to where the file should start.
204	
205	3. To choose the track, select a clip on it. With nothing selected, the file goes on the front track.
206	
207	4. Choose **Edit ▸ Insert at Playhead** or **Edit ▸ Overwrite at Playhead**.
208	
209	</Steps>
210	
211	Neither item has a shortcut. You can also right-click a row and choose either item there, which acts on that row and selects it.
212	
213	The file lands on the [current track](/editing/how-edits-work/#what-an-edit-acts-on). With a [nest](/editing/inside-a-nest/) open, that's a track inside the nest.
214	
215	## Drop with a modifier
216	
217	Drag a row from the Media tab onto a track, and hold a modifier as you let go. Only the keys held at that moment count.
218	
219	| Hold | What the drop does |
220	| --- | --- |
221	| Nothing, or <kbd>⇧</kbd> alone | [Adds the clip](/editing/add-clips/#drag-media-onto-a-track) without moving anything |
222	| <kbd>⌥</kbd> | Inserts at the drop point |
223	| <kbd>⇧⌥</kbd> | Overwrites at the drop point |
224	
225	The modifiers only work on a track. A drop on the preview canvas always [adds the file on a new track](/editing/add-clips/#drop-media-on-the-canvas).
226	
227	## Insert a file
228	
229	Insert keeps everything you've already cut, and the timeline gets longer by the length of the file.
230	
231	- If the point falls inside a clip on the destination track, that clip is split there.
232	- Every unlocked track opens up by the file's length. Clips that start at or after the point move later, and so do markers.
233	- The file lands in the room this makes.
234	
235	Only the destination track is cut. A clip on another track that spans the point stays whole and where it is, so a music bed plays on unbroken under the new file. The exception is a [detached sound](/audio/detach-and-attach/) linked to the clip that was cut. It's cut at the same point, so the pair stays in step.
236	
237	The whole edit is one undo step, Insert.
238	
239	## Overwrite with a file
240	
241	Overwrite moves nothing, and what was there is gone. The timeline only gets longer if the file runs past its end.
242	
243	- The destination track is cut at both ends of the file's length.
244	- Whatever lies between the cuts is removed.
245	- The file lands in the space.
246	
247	Nothing shifts and no other track is touched. The exception is again a detached sound linked to a clip that was cut. It's cut at the same points, and its piece under the new file stays, no longer linked.
248	
249	The whole edit is one undo step, Overwrite.
250	
251	## Good to know
252	
253	- **Locked tracks.** Insert won't work on a locked destination track, because the track can't open up, and the reason appears at the foot of the inspector. Insert elsewhere leaves locked tracks where they are, so their clips can fall out of step with the rest. Overwrite still clears a locked track, because you chose that track and nothing has to move.
254	- **When the menu items are dimmed.** They need a selected row in the Media tab, and that row can't be a `.cube` LUT. A LUT is [applied as a look](/color/luts/), so its right-click **Insert at Playhead** and **Overwrite at Playhead** are dimmed too. A filter that hides the selected row clears the selection.
255	- **The length is the whole file.** Both edits place the file from its first frame to its last. To use part of it, [trim the clip](/editing/trimming/) afterwards. After an Insert, trimming leaves a gap, which [Close Gap](/editing/close-gaps/) removes.
256	
257	## With an agent
258	
259	[`insert_clip`](/mcp/tools-adding-clips/#insert_clip) and [`overwrite_clip`](/mcp/tools-adding-clips/#overwrite_clip) make the same edits. Each takes a track, a file and a time, so an agent doesn't need the playhead or a selected row, and it can place a file inside a nest without opening it. See [Tools: adding clips](/mcp/tools-adding-clips/) and [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/).
260

267	=================== move-clips
268	---
269	title: "Move clips"
270	description: Drag clips along the timeline and between tracks, alone or together, and see what stops a drop.
271	---
272	
273	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
274	
275	Drag a clip to change when it plays or which track it sits on. The clip you see moving while you drag is the real edit, not a stand-in.
276	
277	<AtAGlance
278	  where="Timeline ▸ drag a clip's body"
279	  tools="move_clip"
280	/>
281	
282	## Drag a clip
283	
284	Drag a clip's body left or right to move it in time, and up or down to move it to another track. A clip stops at the start of the timeline.
285	
286	The drag [snaps](/timeline/snapping/) to nearby edits when snapping is on. Hold <kbd>⌘</kbd> during the drag to turn snapping off for that moment.
287	
288	You can't start a drag on a clip on a [locked track](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/).
289	
290	To drag a copy and leave the original, hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> as you press. See [Duplicate clips](/editing/duplicate-clips/).
291	
292	## Move several clips together
293	
294	Select the clips, then drag any one of them. They all move, and they stay the same time and the same number of tracks apart. If the earliest clip reaches the start of the timeline, it stops at 0 and the others keep their distance from it.
295	
296	## Move a clip to a new track
297	
298	Let go above the top lane to make a new track at the front, or below the bottom lane to make a new track at the back. The new track and the move are one undo step.
299	
300	## Clips that come along
301	
302	A clip's linked partner, such as its [detached sound](/audio/detach-and-attach/), moves in time by the same amount and keeps its own track. So you can drag a sound onto a track of its own and its picture stays on its track. A partner on a locked track doesn't move.
303	
304	## Overlaps make a transition
305	
306	If you drop a clip so that it overlaps the clip before it on the track, it gets a Cross Dissolve over the overlap, unless it already has a transition. The overlap has to keep to the [overlap rule](/editing/how-edits-work/#the-overlap-rule).
307	
308	## When a drop won't go where you let go
309	
310	While you drag, the clip only goes where the project allows. Over a position that would break the [overlap rule](/editing/how-edits-work/#the-overlap-rule), it waits at the last position that was allowed, and catches up when you reach one that is.
311	
312	If you let go over a position that isn't allowed, the clip stays at that last allowed position, and a ghost of it slides there from where you let go. If it never reached an allowed position, it's back where it started and nothing has changed. There's no beep and no message.
313	
314	## One undo step per drag
315	
316	A whole drag is one undo step, however long it lasts. **Edit ▸ Undo** (<kbd>⌘Z</kbd>) names it Move Clips. A click that doesn't move the clip adds no undo step.
317	
318	## Good to know
319	
320	- A locked clip that's part of a selection moves with the others if you start the drag on an unlocked clip.
321	- Clips selected on more than one track can't make a new track at the front. Let go above the top lane and they stay at the last allowed position. Below the bottom lane works.
322	- With 64 tracks in the project, there's no new track to make. A drop above or below the lanes moves the clips in time only.
323	- To shift clips by an exact number of frames, [nudge them](/editing/nudge-clips/).
324	
325	## With an agent
326	
327	`move_clip` takes the clips and how far to shift them, where a negative shift moves them earlier. Give it a track to move them there as well, and leave that out to keep them on their tracks. Like a drag, it won't break the overlap rule. See [Tools: moving and trimming](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#move_clip).
328	
329	## Related

333	- [Nudge clips](/editing/nudge-clips/)

335	=================== nudge-clips
336	---
337	title: "Nudge clips"
338	description: Move the selected clips one or ten frames at a time from the keyboard.
339	---
340	
341	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
342	
343	A nudge moves the selected clips by an exact number of frames, for the small corrections that are hard to make with a drag.
344	
345	<AtAGlance keys={[',', '.', '⇧,', '⇧.']} tools="move_clip" />
346	
347	## Nudge the selection
348	
349	| Keys | Moves the selection |
350	| --- | --- |
351	| <kbd>,</kbd> | One frame earlier |
352	| <kbd>.</kbd> | One frame later |
353	| <kbd>⇧,</kbd> | Ten frames earlier |
354	| <kbd>⇧.</kbd> | Ten frames later |
355	
356	On a US keyboard, <kbd>⇧,</kbd> and <kbd>⇧.</kbd> are the keys that type `<` and `>`.
357	
358	Each press is one undo step, Nudge Clips. These keys have no <kbd>⌘</kbd>, so while a text field has the focus they type into it instead. See [Keys and typing](/getting-started/keys-and-typing/).
359	
360	## Good to know
361	
362	A nudge is an ordinary [move](/editing/move-clips/), with the same rules:
363	
364	- It beeps with nothing selected.
365	- A nudge that would break the [overlap rule](/editing/how-edits-work/#the-overlap-rule) beeps and changes nothing, and the reason appears at the foot of the inspector. A nudge that lands on a small enough overlap makes a Cross Dissolve.
366	- The earliest clip stops at the start of the timeline, so <kbd>⇧,</kbd> on a clip three frames from the start moves it three frames. A clip already at the start beeps.
367	- A linked partner on an unlocked track moves with its clip.
368	
369	Unlike a drag, a nudge moves a selected clip on a [locked track](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/). It doesn't snap, and it never changes a clip's track.
370	
371	## With an agent
372	
373	An agent nudges with `move_clip`, giving the shift as a time. See [Tools: moving and trimming](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#move_clip).
374

380	=================== trimming
381	---
382	title: "Trim clips"
383	description: Shorten or lengthen a clip by dragging an edge, trimming to the playhead or typing a time.
384	---
385	
386	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
387	
388	Trimming changes where a clip starts or ends without moving the footage inside it. Use it to take the slack off a shot, or to pull back in what you cut too tightly.
389	
390	<AtAGlance
391	  menu={['Clip ▸ Trim Start to Playhead', 'Clip ▸ Trim End to Playhead']}
392	  keys={['W', 'E']}
393	  where={[
394	    'Timeline ▸ drag a clip edge',
395	    'The Trim Start to Playhead and Trim End to Playhead buttons in the timeline bar',
396	    'Clip tab ▸ Clip ▸ Timing ▸ In and Out',
397	  ]}
398	  tools={['trim_start', 'trim_end']}
399	/>
400	
401	## Drag an edge
402	
403	Drag either edge of a clip. The edge is the outer 7 points of the clip. The pointer becomes a left-right resize cursor there, and a selected clip shows trim grips.
404	
405	- **A clip 21 points wide or less** on screen is all body, so [zoom in](/timeline/zoom-and-scroll/) to trim it.
406	- **Clips on locked tracks** have no edges to grab and show no resize cursor. <kbd>W</kbd>, <kbd>E</kbd> and the **In** and **Out** fields still trim one, if you've selected it by clicking.
407	- **A fade handle or an action band** under the pointer takes the press before the edge does.
408	
409	The drag [snaps](/timeline/snapping/) when snapping is on, and holding <kbd>⌘</kbd> turns snapping off for that moment. The whole drag is one undo step, Trim Clip.
410	
411	Hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> as you press a media clip's end edge to [rate stretch](/speed/rate-stretch/) it instead, which changes its speed to fill the new length. <kbd>⌥</kbd> on the start edge is an ordinary trim. <kbd>⌥⇧</kbd> on either edge is a [roll](/editing/slip-and-roll/).
412	
413	## What each edge does
414	
415	**A start trim** moves the clip's start and its place in the footage together. The frame under the edge stays put, and the rest of the clip stays where it is on the timeline.
416	
417	**An end trim** moves the clip's end. Nothing else about the clip changes.
418	
419	Neither trim moves the clips around it, so a trim leaves a gap or fills one. If you pull a clip over its neighbour, the overlap has to keep to the [overlap rule](/editing/how-edits-work/#the-overlap-rule). Where it does, the later clip gets a Cross Dissolve over the overlap, unless it already has a transition. Where it doesn't, a dragged edge waits at the last position that was allowed, and <kbd>W</kbd>, <kbd>E</kbd> or a typed time beeps and changes nothing.
420	
421	## Trim to the playhead
422	
423	Select the clips, move the playhead inside them, then press <kbd>W</kbd> to trim their starts to the playhead or <kbd>E</kbd> to trim their ends. **Clip ▸ Trim Start to Playhead**, **Clip ▸ Trim End to Playhead** and the matching buttons in the timeline bar do the same.
424	
425	Each selected clip the playhead is inside is trimmed, as one undo step: Trim Start for <kbd>W</kbd> and Trim End for <kbd>E</kbd>.
426	
427	When no selected clip crosses the playhead, the menu items are greyed out and the keys beep. The menu doesn't show <kbd>W</kbd> and <kbd>E</kbd> beside its items, but the buttons' tooltips name them.
428	
429	## Type a time
430	
431	Select one clip and open the **Timing** section of the Clip tab's **Clip** sub-tab. **In** is where the clip starts on the timeline and **Out** is where it ends. Typing a new time is the same trim as dragging that edge.
432	
433	A time past what the clip can reach lands at the limit, and the field shows where it went. See [Type a clip's timing](/editing/timing-section/).
434	
435	## How far a trim goes
436	
437	A clip always keeps at least one frame.
438	
439	A media clip's trim stops at the start and end of its file. The end stops on the last whole frame the file still holds. A [slip or a roll](/editing/slip-and-roll/) can't pass either end of the file either.
440	
441	Pictures, freeze frames, text, shapes, graphics, adjustment clips and nests have no file length, so they trim to any length. A trimmed [nest](/editing/nests/) cuts nothing inside it. Trimming its end hides the tail. A nest always plays from its own first frame, so trimming its start moves what's inside along with the new start, rather than cutting into it.
442	
443	## What a trim keeps
444	
445	- **Linked sound.** Trim a picture and its [detached sound](/audio/detach-and-attach/) follows, if the two edges matched and the sound's track isn't locked. Trim the sound half and it goes alone, which is how you make a [J-cut or an L-cut](/audio/j-and-l-cuts/). <kbd>W</kbd> and <kbd>E</kbd> work the same way. The **In** and **Out** fields always take a matching partner along, whichever half you selected.
446	- **Actions.** They keep their time from the clip's start, so they stay put relative to the new start. An action past a new end is kept, and only the part inside the clip plays. See [How edits move actions](/motion/how-edits-move-actions/).
447	- **Caption words.** Timed words stay on their speech.
448	- **Speed ramps.** On a [ramped clip](/speed/edit-a-ramped-clip/), the ramp stays where it is in the clip, so what plays after a new start can change. The start stops where the clip still fits its media.
449	
450	## Trim a graphic
451	
452	Trimming the front of a graphic clip cuts into its animation. The **In** row of the **Timeline** section in the **Graphic** sub-tab moves forward, and the outro keeps its timing. That **In** counts the graphic's own frames, so it isn't the **In** field under **Timing**.
453	
454	A graphic has no file to run out of, so you can also drag its start back earlier. The graphic's **In** stops at 0, and the clip keeps growing.
455	
456	Trimming the end leaves a pinned **Length** alone. With **Follow Clip** on, the graphic's own timeline ends at the clip's new end. A clip longer than a pinned **Length** keeps drawing frames past it, with its progress held at the end. See [Graphic size and timing](/graphics/size-and-timing/).
457	
458	## With an agent
459	
460	[`trim_start`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#trim_start) and [`trim_end`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#trim_end) move an edge to a time you give them. With `alone`, they trim either half of a linked pair on its own. On the timeline, only the sound half trims alone. See [Tools: moving and trimming](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/).
461

470	---
471	title: "Type a clip's timing"
472	description: "Trim a clip to an exact time by typing its In and Out, and read its length, in the Clip tab's Timing section."
473	---
474	
475	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
476	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
477	
478	The Timing section is for when you know the number. Type where a clip starts and ends on the timeline, and read how long it is, without dragging an edge.
479	
480	<AtAGlance
481	  where="Clip tab ▸ Clip ▸ Timing"
482	  tools={['trim_start', 'trim_end']}
483	/>
484	
485	## Type In and Out
486	
487	<Steps>
488	
489	1. Select one clip.
490	
491	2. In the [inspector's](/getting-started/inspector/) **Clip** tab, choose the **Clip** sub-tab, the last one. **Timing** is its first section, and it starts shut. Click its header to open it, and it stays open until you shut it. Shut, the header still shows the clip's length.
492	
493	3. Click **In** or **Out** and type a time. `1:23`, `83.5` and `1:23:04` all work, as they do in the toolbar's time field. See [Inspector fields](/getting-started/inspector-fields/).
494	
495	4. Press <kbd>Return</kbd> or <kbd>Tab</kbd>.
496	
497	</Steps>
498	
499	| Field | What it is | What typing does |
500	| --- | --- | --- |
501	| **In** | Where the clip starts on the timeline | Trims its front edge. The rest of the clip stays where it is. |
502	| **Out** | Where the clip ends on the timeline | Trims its back edge. |
503	
504	Both are positions on the timeline, not positions in the file. A later **In** hides the start of the footage, and an earlier one brings it back. To move the whole clip without trimming it, [drag it](/editing/move-clips/) instead.
505	
506	Each change is one undo step, named Trim Start or Trim End. The time lands on the project's frame grid.
507	
508	## How far an edge can go
509	
510	A number out of range doesn't beep. The edge goes as far as it can, and the field shows where it landed.
511	
512	| Field | Earliest | Latest |
513	| --- | --- | --- |
514	| **In** | The start of the timeline, or as far back as the file has footage | One frame before the clip's end |
515	| **Out** | One frame after the clip's start | As far as the file has footage |
516	
517	Only a clip that plays a video or audio file has a footage limit. Text, shapes, pictures and graphics have no file length to run out of.
518	
519	Three things leave the clip as it was:
520	
521	- If you type a new value but it puts the edge where it already is, Frame Job beeps.
522	- If the text can't be read as a time, Frame Job beeps and the field goes back to the old value.
523	- If the new edge would break the [overlap rule](/getting-started/refused-edits/), Frame Job beeps and gives the reason at the foot of the inspector.
524	
525	An overlap the rule allows goes through, and the clip that now overlaps the one before it gets a Cross Dissolve.
526	
527	## Read the duration
528	
529	**Duration** shows the clip's length, in the project's [timecode style](/projects/background-and-timecode/). You can't type in it: change the length through **In** and **Out**.
530	
531	## With several clips selected
532	
533	**In**, **Out** and **Duration** each describe one clip, so they go away when you select more than one.
534	
535	If every selected clip plays a video or audio file, Timing stays and holds only the [Reverse](/speed/reverse/) rows, which apply to all of them as one undo step. Its header shows the lengths of the selected clips added together, followed by "total".
536	
537	If the selection also holds anything else, such as text, a shape, a picture or a freeze frame, there's no Timing section.
538	
539	## Good to know
540	
541	- With one clip selected, the Reverse rows appear under **Duration** only for a clip that plays a video or audio file.
542	- Typing an edge also moves the same edge of a [linked clip](/audio/detach-and-attach/) when the two line up and its track isn't locked. That holds even when you type on the sound half. To move a sound's edge without its picture, [use a drag, <kbd>W</kbd> or <kbd>E</kbd>](/editing/slip-and-roll/#move-a-sound-clips-edge-alone).
543	- A locked track stops drags, not these fields. If a clip on a locked track is selected, typing still trims it.
544	- Inside a [nest](/editing/nests/), the times count from the nest's own start.
545	- [Actions](/motion/how-edits-move-actions/) keep their place measured from the clip's start, so trimming the front edge moves them along the timeline with it.
546	
547	## With an agent
548	
549	[`trim_start`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#trim_start) and [`trim_end`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#trim_end) move the same two edges to a time on the timeline, and stop at the same limits. With `alone`, the edge moves without its linked partner's. See [Tools: moving and trimming](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/).
550

557	=================== slip-and-roll
558	---
559	title: "Slip and roll"
560	description: "Change which footage a clip shows, or move the cut between two clips, without moving anything else on the timeline."
561	---
562	
563	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
564	
565	Slip and roll are for fine-tuning once your clips are where they belong. A slip changes which part of the file a clip shows. A roll moves the cut between two clips. Neither moves any other clip.
566	
567	<AtAGlance
568	  keys={['⌥⇧-drag body', '⌥⇧-drag edge']}
569	  where="The timeline"
570	  tools={['slip', 'roll', 'trim_start', 'trim_end']}
571	/>
572	
573	## Slip a clip
574	
575	Hold <kbd>⌥⇧</kbd> and drag the body of a clip. The clip stays where it is at the same length, and the footage slides underneath it. Drag right to show later footage and left to show earlier footage.
576	
577	The whole drag is one undo step, named Slip. It doesn't change the selection, so you can slip a clip without selecting it.
578	
579	- A slip stops when the clip reaches either end of its file, and keeps what it reached. It doesn't turn into a trim. If there's no footage to slide into, the drag changes nothing.
580	- It moves in whole frames and never snaps, because the timeline's snap points mean nothing inside the footage.
581	- The footage moves at the clip's speed. At ×2, dragging one frame slides the footage two frames.
582	- A [freeze frame](/speed/freeze-frame/) slips too, which changes the frame it holds. It stops one frame short of the end of its file.
583	- A linked sound clip on an unlocked track slips with its picture, so the two stay in sync. They move by the smaller of the two distances they each have room for.
584	
585	Only clips that play a file have footage to slide. The drag does nothing on text, a shape, a picture, a graphic or a nest.
586	
587	## Roll a cut
588	
589	Hold <kbd>⌥⇧</kbd> and drag a clip's edge, the outer 7 points of the clip. The cut moves: one clip gets longer and the other gets shorter by the same amount, and the outer edges of the pair stay where they are.
590	
591	| Edge you drag | Cut that moves |
592	| --- | --- |
593	| The clip's start | The cut with the clip before it |
594	| The clip's end | The cut with the clip after it |
595	
596	The whole drag is one undo step, named Roll.
597	
598	- A roll [snaps](/timeline/snapping/) like a trim. Hold <kbd>⌘</kbd> during the drag to stop snapping.
599	- Each clip keeps at least one frame.
600	- A clip that plays a file can't grow past what the file has. Text, shapes and pictures have no such limit.
601	- A roll needs two clips that touch exactly. With a gap at that edge there's no cut to move, and with an overlap there's a [transition](/motion/transition-settings/), whose length you set in its own section. Either way the drag does nothing.
602	- A clip 21 points wide or less on screen has no edges to grab, and the drag slips it instead. [Zoom in](/timeline/zoom-and-scroll/) first.
603	
604	When you roll a picture's cut, a linked sound clip rolls with it, as long as it starts at the same point, it touches a clip before it, and its track is unlocked.
605	
606	## Move a sound clip's edge alone
607	
608	A [detached sound clip](/audio/detach-and-attach/) that's still linked to its picture can move an edge on its own. This is how a [J-cut or L-cut](/audio/j-and-l-cuts/) is made. These move only the sound's edge and leave the picture where it is:
609	
610	- Drag the sound clip's edge.
611	- Select it and press <kbd>W</kbd> or <kbd>E</kbd> to [trim it to the playhead](/editing/trimming/).
612	- Hold <kbd>⌥⇧</kbd> and drag the sound clip's edge to roll its cut.
613	
614	It works in that direction only. Trimming or rolling the picture's edge also moves the sound's edge when the two line up, and a slip always takes both.
615	
616	## What happens to actions and timed words
617	
618	A slip leaves [actions](/motion/how-edits-move-actions/) where they are, because only the footage inside the clip moves.
619	
620	A roll leaves each clip's actions at the same distance from that clip's start. So on the clip after the cut, the actions move with the cut along the timeline. On the clip before it, they stay put, and if that clip gets shorter it can end before an action does.
621	
622	Timed caption words are the exception. They stay on the speech they time, so a roll doesn't shift them against the sound. A [graphic](/graphics/size-and-timing/) after the cut stays in step too: its **In** moves with the cut.
623	
624	## Good to know
625	
626	- Neither gesture works on a locked track. The drag does nothing. A linked clip on a locked track stays put while the clip you drag moves.
627	- On a clip with a [speed ramp](/speed/edit-a-ramped-clip/), the actions stay where they are and the limits come from the ramp, so a cut stops rolling where the clip would no longer fit its file.
628	
629	## With an agent
630	
631	[`slip`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#slip) takes a clip and how far to slide, and a positive distance shows later footage. Where the drag does nothing on text, a shape, a picture, a graphic or a nest, the tool gives an error.
632	
633	[`roll`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#roll) takes the clip to the right of the cut and the time the cut moves to. If no clip on the track ends where that clip begins, it gives an error saying so.
634	
635	With `alone`, `roll` moves a picture's cut and leaves a lined-up linked sound on an unlocked track where it is. No gesture can do that. [`trim_start`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#trim_start) and [`trim_end`](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/#trim_end) take `alone` too, to move one clip's edge without its partner's. See [Tools: moving and trimming](/mcp/tools-move-and-trim/).

643	=================== splitting
644	---
645	title: "Split clips"
646	description: "Cut clips in two at the playhead, and see what each piece keeps of the footage, actions, word timings and graphics."
647	---
648	
649	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
650	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
651	
652	Split cuts a clip in two at the playhead, so you can trim, move or remove one piece without touching the other.
653	
654	<AtAGlance
655	  menu="Clip ▸ Split"
656	  keys="⌘T"
657	  where="The scissors button in the timeline bar"
658	  tools="split"
659	/>
660	
661	## Split at the playhead
662	
663	<Steps>
664	
665	1. Move the playhead to the frame you want to cut on.
666	
667	2. Select the clips to cut, or select nothing to cut everything under the playhead.
668	
669	3. Press <kbd>⌘T</kbd>, choose **Clip ▸ Split**, or click the scissors button in the timeline bar.
670	
671	</Steps>
672	
673	| What's selected | What gets cut |
674	| --- | --- |
675	| One or more clips | Each selected clip the playhead is inside |
676	| Nothing | Every clip under the playhead on every unlocked track |
677	
678	It's one undo step, named Split, however many clips it cuts. The command is available whenever the timeline has clips.
679	
680	The playhead has to be strictly inside a clip. A playhead sitting exactly on a clip's edge is at a cut already, so that clip is left alone. If nothing can be cut, Frame Job beeps and nothing changes.
681	
682	A clip on a locked track is left alone when nothing is selected, but it's still cut if you selected it.
683	
684	## Footage stays continuous
685	
686	The second piece carries on playing the footage from where the first stopped, at the same speed, so the split doesn't show when you play it back. If an action is animating the clip, the second piece starts from where that animation had got to at the cut, such as its position or volume. It keeps the clip's name, label and settings.
687	
688	On a clip with a [speed ramp](/speed/edit-a-ramped-clip/), the two pieces meet at exactly the same point in the footage, and the second starts at the rate in force at the cut.
689	
690	## Linked sound
691	
692	A [linked clip](/audio/detach-and-attach/) on an unlocked track is cut too, when the playhead is inside it, and the two second halves are linked to each other.
693	
694	If the linked clip isn't cut, because its track is locked or the playhead isn't inside it, it stays linked to whichever piece shares more of its time. The other piece isn't linked to anything.
695	
696	## Actions and word timings
697	
698	[Actions](/motion/how-edits-move-actions/) stay with the piece they fall in:
699	
700	- An action that ends at or before the cut stays on the first piece.
701	- An action that starts at or after the cut moves to the second piece.
702	- An action that spans the cut becomes two. The first half ends at the value it had reached at the cut, and the second carries on to the original target, so the join doesn't show. Both keep the action's curve.
703	
704	An [entrance and exit preset](/motion/entrances-and-exits/) is tied to the clip's ends, so the first piece keeps the entrance and the second keeps the exit. A [text reveal](/text-and-shapes/text-reveal/) divides the same way. Otherwise the clip would leave at the cut and arrive again on the far side of it.
705	
706	Caption word timings stay on their words. Both pieces keep the full text, the first with its timings as they were and the second with its timings moved to match its new start.
707	
708	The one exception is a text clip whose wording an action changes. If the second piece's text at the cut no longer has the same number of words as its timings, the second piece loses its word timings and shows its text all at once.
709	
710	## Split a graphic
711	
712	A [graphic](/graphics/size-and-timing/) carries on across the cut rather than starting again, and plays its outro once, at the true end.
713	
714	The graphic's **In** on the second piece starts at the cut, so it picks up where the first piece left off. Both pieces keep the original's **Length**, so an outro still plays at the same moment. That pins the length, so **Follow Clip** is off on both pieces afterwards.
715	
716	Trimming the start of a graphic, or [rolling the cut](/editing/slip-and-roll/#roll-a-cut) before it, moves **In** in the same way. Trimming the end leaves a pinned **Length** alone. With **Follow Clip** on, the graphic's own timeline ends at the new end.
717	
718	## Good to know
719	
720	- The cut lands on the project's frame grid.
721	- A [transition](/motion/transitions/) into the clip stays on the first piece. The second piece starts with a hard cut.
722	- [Sound fades](/audio/fades/) are copied to both pieces. A clip with a fade-in fades in again at the cut, and one with a fade-out dips at the cut, so set them again on the side of the cut where you don't want them.
723	- A project holds up to 4,096 clips. A split that would pass that shows an error alert, and nothing changes.
724	
725	## With an agent
726	
727	`split` cuts at a time you give it, or at the playhead if you leave the time out. Give it a list of clips to cut those, or leave the list out to cut every clip on an unlocked track at that time, as the menu item does with nothing selected. See [Tools: cutting and deleting](/mcp/tools-cut-and-delete/#split).
